youtube_title: Bass Lake, Indiana: the monster that smashed a fishing boat (1838 and 1893)
youtube:
You asked for Bass Lake! In 1838, when Bass Lake in Starke County was called Cedar Lake, a Logansport paper printed a legend: a monster had been killed on its banks, its bones could still be found, and its mate escaped into the water. In 1893, newspapers said four men went fishing on the lake one morning, among them the sheriff and George Scoville, a lawyer who defended President Garfield's assassin. One of them hooked something that towed their boat for half an hour, then surfaced and smashed the stern with its tail, throwing the two men standing there into the water. They said it was forty feet long, greenish-black, with a huge pointed head. Bass Lake sits on a ridge with no stream flowing in; springs and wells help fill it. Comment your town, and it could be next! #BassLake #StarkeCounty #Indiana #LakeMonster #Legend #LaPorteAfterDark #Shorts

All pictures are drawn; no one is shown hurt. Narration is a computer voice. Sources: The Evening Herald (Shenandoah, Pa.), "Cedar Bass Lake's Monster," June 22, 1893, p. 2, via the Pennsylvania Newspaper Archive; New Orleans Daily Picayune, May 18, 1893, as listed in Charles Fort's notes; Donald Smalley, "The Logansport Telegraph and the Monster of the Indiana Lakes," Indiana Magazine of History (1946), quoting the Logansport Herald, Aug. 16, 1838; Ray E. Boomhower, "The Father of Indiana History and the Lake Monster" (2020); T. H. Ball, Northwestern Indiana from 1800 to 1900 (1900); Starke County History Center, "Mysterious Bass Lake"; Bass Lake Conservancy District; Only In Your State; National Park Service (George Scoville and the Guiteau trial). note: Viewer request passed along by Scoop, Nov. 16, 2026 ('bass lake'). A legend (1838) and a newspaper story (1893), told as what the papers said.
factcheck: Three independent checks Nov. 16, 2026 (script, on-screen text and pictures only; the third on the changes). The first couldn't open page 2 of the 1893 Evening Herald and relied on a 2024 blog; the page's OCR confirms the headline 'CEDAR BASS LAKE'S MONSTER', 'a free ride for half an hour', 'smashing the stern in a thousand pieces', 'its head is huge and pointed', 'greenish black', forty feet by three, no visible fins, 'Sheriff Vanderweele, of Knox' and Scoville as the attorney who defended Garfield's murderer. Fixes: 'One hooked something that towed their boat'; one boat of four men (two thrown off the stern, two aboard until it sank near shore), morning light, a hand line and a line made fast instead of rods, the creature as a long finless body (not a raised neck with humps), the opening boat going down; line 7 'Bass Lake sits on a ridge with no stream flowing in. Springs and wells help fill it.' (Blatchley and Ashley 1900; Starke County History Center; Bass Lake Conservancy District); label 'CEDAR LAKE (NOW BASS LAKE)' (the 1838 Herald: 'is now called Cedar lake'); the card names Shenandoah, Pa. 'The papers' rests on the Evening Herald plus Charles Fort's notes (New Orleans Picayune, May 18, and Philadelphia Public Ledger, May 17, 1893). Third check: all supported.
